module_title: Irrevocable Licenses, Quasi-Easements & The 2001 Registration Amendment
introduction: Tailored for advanced legal exams and UPSC Law Optional, this level explores complex property nuances. It details when a simple license becomes absolutely irrevocable, the strict doctrine of Easement of Necessity, and the monumental 2001 Amendment that changed how Section 49 interacts with the TPA.

core_concepts.title: Easement of Necessity vs. Quasi-Easement (Section 13)
core_concepts.description:
- Easement of Necessity: Arises when a single property is divided and sold, and one part becomes completely landlocked. The law implies a right of way over the other part. It only arises in cases of **absolute necessity** (there is literally no other way out). It extinguishes the moment an alternative route is found.
- Quasi-Easement: Arises for the comfortable and continuous enjoyment of the property as it was enjoyed *before* the division. It must be continuous and apparent. It is not an absolute necessity, but necessary for reasonable enjoyment.

core_concepts.title: When a License becomes Irrevocable (Section 60, Easements Act)
core_concepts.description:
Generally, a license can be revoked at any time by the grantor. However, Section 60 provides two strict exceptions where it becomes irrevocable:
1. If it is coupled with a transfer of property and such transfer is in force (e.g., A sells B timber growing on A's land. B's license to enter A's land to cut the timber cannot be revoked).
2. If the licensee, acting upon the license, has **executed a work of a permanent character and incurred expenses** in doing so (e.g., A allows B to build a permanent brick house on A's land. A cannot later revoke the license and demolish the house).

core_concepts.title: Extinction of Easements (Sections 37-47)
core_concepts.description:
An easement can be legally extinguished in several ways:
1. Release: Express or implied release by the dominant owner.
2. Unity of Ownership: If the dominant and servient heritage are bought by the exact same person, the easement is extinguished (you cannot have an easement over your own land).
3. Non-Enjoyment: If an easement is not used for an unbroken period of **20 years**, it is extinguished (Sec 47).

core_concepts.title: The 2001 Registration Amendment (Interaction with TPA Sec 53A)
core_concepts.description:
A highly advanced, heavily tested concept.
- Prior to 2001: Under the Doctrine of Part Performance (Sec 53A TPA), a buyer could protect their possession using an *unregistered* agreement to sell.
- The 2001 Amendment: The Registration Act and TPA were amended. Now, an agreement to sell immovable property MUST be registered. If the agreement to sell is unregistered, the buyer **CANNOT use Section 53A as a shield** to protect their possession in court. The protection of Part Performance is totally gone for unregistered agreements post-2001.

important_entities.name: Customary Easements (Section 18)
important_entities.key_fact: Easements acquired by virtue of local custom.
important_entities.significance: Distinct from prescriptive easements, customary easements apply to a specific locality or community, not just a single dominant owner. For example, a custom in a village allowing all residents to hold a specific festival on a particular piece of private land, or a right to bury the dead in a specific place.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: If an exam says: 'A divides his land. He can reach the main road via a long, muddy 2km path, but going through B's portion takes only 100 meters. Can A claim an Easement of Necessity?' **NO**. The Supreme Court has ruled that an easement of necessity is based on *absolute* necessity. Mere convenience or a shorter route does not create an easement of necessity.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: R U N (Release, Unity of Ownership, Non-enjoyment)
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Remember the three main ways an established easement is legally destroyed.

exam_strategy_tips: In UPSC Mains, when discussing the Doctrine of Part Performance, you MUST explicitly state that the 2001 Amendment to Section 49 of the Registration Act made the registration of the 'Agreement to Sell' mandatory for invoking Section 53A of the TPA.
